terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, with the infinitive
evidence: Cic. Sen. 25: nec vērō dubitat agricola … respondēre
terms.comment: With an infinitive dubitāre is “to hesitate to do”, most often with a negative (nōn dubitō, “I don’t hesitate to”) or in a question (quid dubitās?, “why are you hesitating?”). Its other sense, “to doubt”, is in doubt. sine dubitātiōne is “without hesitation”.

evidence: Cic. Att. 10.8.5: assequor omnia sī properō, sī cūnctor āmittō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To be slow to act, from caution or reluctance: Fabius was Cūnctātor. The noun is cūnctātiō (Cic. Amic. 44).

terms.gloss: hesitate, be at a loss; falter in speech
evidence: Cic. Ac. 2.52: dubitant, haesitant, revocant sē interdum (Lewis & Short)
Cic. de Or. 1.115: linguā haesitantēs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Properly “to stick fast” (see stuck); then to be stuck for what to do or say, uncertain, at a loss.

phrases.latin: nec vērō dubitat agricola, quamvīs sit senex, quaerentī cui serat respondēre: ‘dīs immortālibus’
phrases.english: nor does the farmer, old as he is, hesitate to answer anyone who asks whom he is planting for: ‘for the immortal gods’

phrases.latin: cūnctātī aliquamdiū sunt, dum alius alium, ut proelium incipiant, circumspectant
phrases.english: they hung back for a while, each looking round at the others to start the fight
let there always be eagerness, and no hanging back

phrases.latin: quid dubitāmus pultāre atque hūc ēvocāre ambōs forās?
phrases.english: why are we hesitating to knock and call them both out here?

sources: Lewis & Short: dubito · Lewis & Short: cunctor · Lewis & Short: haesito
Cicero (Sen. 25, Amic. 44) and Livy from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-livius); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.
